title: Growing, Growing, Growing
subtitle: Exponential Expressions and Exponential Functions, Non-Linear Functions

aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master middle school math teacher.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: Below is a student's mathematics document, as a text summary, a picture, or both. Either may be absent. Evaluate and categorize it.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: Return exactly one item: a single sentence of at most 30 words, written to the student as "you", saying why this category fits by naming one specific thing in their document - a number, ratio, label, table column, or phrase they actually wrote. Do not restate the problem, summarize the document as a whole, or explain the mathematics in general.

GGG 3.1 Making Smaller Ballots: Introducing Exponential Decay
GGG 4.1 Looking for Patterns among Exponents

aiUnitSummary.overview: Growing, Growing, Growing is a grade 8 unit on exponential functions, set against the linear functions students already know. Investigation 1 builds the form y = a(b^x) from repeated doubling — paper cut in half again and again, grains on a chessboard, a plant covering a lake — identifying the growth factor b and the initial value a as the y-intercept, and introducing exponential and scientific notation as the numbers outgrow standard form. Investigation 2 moves to fractional growth factors and connects them to percent growth rates, where a 6% increase is a factor of 1.06 and the increase compounds. Investigation 3 turns to decay, where the factor lies between 0 and 1, through medicine clearing the bloodstream and water cooling toward room temperature, then examines how a and b shape the graph. Investigation 4 works on the exponent properties themselves, extending them to zero, negative and rational exponents and to arithmetic in scientific notation.

entries.problemDigest: An orientation activity for the CLUE environment rather than mathematics. It covers the group model of up to four students, how to change groups, the tab structure of a problem, and the tools and collaboration features students will use for the rest of the unit. It carries no mathematical content forward.

entries.priorKnowledge: From earlier units: linear relationships represented by tables, graphs and equations, with a constant rate of change and a y-intercept; plotting points; writing an equation from a pattern. From Number Connections: repeated multiplication and powers. Exponential relationships are introduced here.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the unit by contrasting a doubling pattern with a linear one. Chen halves a sheet of paper, stacks the pieces and halves again, recording the number of ballots after each cut, and looks for a pattern that predicts the count after any number of cuts. Students describe the growth pattern and represent it in a table, a graph and an equation. The What If section asks what each representation is good for, how to predict the count after 20 cuts and the cuts needed for 500 ballots — which the table cannot reach conveniently — and where the doubling shows up in each representation. The closing comparison with linear relationships is the point: the number of ballots is multiplied rather than increased by a fixed amount.
entries.approachGuidance: Table, graph and equation are compared for what each makes easy or hard, with no single right tool. Support moving between them rather than settling on one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential growth as repeated multiplication by a constant factor; representing a relationship with a table, graph and equation; linear functions for contrast; from Number Connections, exponential form, base, exponent, and standard against expanded form.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces exponential form and the vocabulary of exponential functions through the chessboard story: one ruba on the first square, two on the second, doubling across all 64. Students write the relationship as an equation in which the number of squares is the exponent. The What If section sets Chen's and Kayla's competing equations against each other and asks which is right, what each gives when n = 1, what the growth factor is and what the y-intercept of the graph is — the disagreement turning on whether the exponent is n or n − 1, which is exactly where the initial value sits. Alternative reward plans from the king and queen are then compared, including ones that are linear rather than exponential.
entries.approachGuidance: Two defensible-looking equations are set against each other and the resolution is about where the initial value sits. Support the argument rather than naming the correct equation.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential functions written as an equation with a growth factor and a y-intercept; exponential form and standard form; tables and graphs of exponential growth; reading a calculator display; place value for large numbers.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces scientific notation and y-intercepts other than 1. A water plant covering 1,000 square feet of a 25,000,000-square-foot lake doubles monthly, so the initial value is 1,000 rather than 1; students decide whether the relationship is exponential, find the coverage after a year, and work out when the lake is completely covered. Scientific notation is introduced because the numbers exceed what a calculator shows in standard form, with students converting both ways. The What If section matches expressions to the month each represents, and then has students read a snake population off an exponential graph and write its equation, explaining what information the graph supplies.
entries.approachGuidance: Students may work from the table, the graph or the equation to find when the lake is covered. Follow their chosen representation.

entries.priorKnowledge: The equation form of an exponential function with a growth factor and an initial value; that the y-intercept is the initial value; scientific notation and converting to standard form; reading values from an exponential table or graph.
entries.problemDigest: Focuses on reading an equation rather than building one. Given m = 50(3^d) for the area of mould after d days, students identify the starting area, the growth factor, the area after 5 days and the day the area reaches 6,400 square millimetres — so the same equation is interrogated in both directions, forwards for a value and backwards for a time. The What If section has students write the equation for algae growth from a table and compare it with the mould equation, then find the day the algae reaches an area given in scientific notation. A further situation practises producing and reading calculator displays in scientific notation.
entries.approachGuidance: Working backwards from a value to a time can be done by table, graph or reasoning with the equation. Support the method the student chooses.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential functions with whole-number growth factors; the equation form with initial value and growth factor; tables, graphs and scientific notation; writing an equation from a table; linear functions for contrast.
entries.problemDigest: Moves to growth factors that are not whole numbers. From a table of rabbit population data students write an equation for the population after n years, explaining what in the table they used, then predict the population at 10, 25 and 50 years and find when it exceeds a billion. The What If section introduces doubling time using p = 15(1.2)^n: students identify the growth factor and initial population, find how long the population takes to double, then check whether the doubling time starting from year 3 and from year 10 is the same — which it is, and that invariance is the result the problem is after. The Rule of 72 is offered afterwards as a check against their findings.
entries.approachGuidance: Doubling time can be found from a table, a graph or by trial with the equation. Support the student's route and the generalisation they draw.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential functions with fractional growth factors; initial value and growth factor in an equation; doubling time; percent increase and finding a percent of an amount; that a growth factor is the ratio of consecutive values.
entries.problemDigest: Connects the growth factor to a percent growth rate. A $5,000 bond increasing by 6% a year must be valued at 18 years, which requires recognising that a 6% increase is multiplication by 1.06. The What If section compares several family members' approaches, including a table, and asks students to judge them, then follows Sam's exploration of a 7% rate written as 5,000 × 1.07^4 — asking whether that makes sense, what the value is at 18, and how long various targets take. The relationship between rate and factor, that the factor is one plus the rate, is the problem's content, and the growth factor is also described as the ratio of each year's value to the previous one.
entries.approachGuidance: Several family strategies are compared and students judge each. Support evaluating a strategy rather than replacing it with the compound-interest formula.

entries.priorKnowledge: Growth factor and growth rate and the relationship between them; exponential equations with an initial value; that percent increase compounds on the new total; reading tables and graphs of exponential growth; distinguishing linear from exponential patterns.
entries.problemDigest: Separates the roles of initial value and growth factor, and names compound growth — the increase from year to year grows because the percent is taken on the new total. Students examine several tables of projected antelope populations, describe the growth in each, decide which if any shows 3% annual growth, and classify each relationship as linear, exponential or neither. The What If section helps a student who cannot find the starting value from a table, examines another's graph-based strategy, and gives a calculation written as 2,000 × 1.05 × 1.05 × 1.05 × 1.05 from which students must read off the initial value, growth rate, growth factor and number of years.
entries.approachGuidance: Deciding whether a table is linear, exponential or neither admits several lines of argument. Support the reasoning rather than the classification alone.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential growth with whole-number and fractional growth factors; initial value, growth factor and growth rate; tables, graphs and equations of exponential functions; from 1.1, the ballot-cutting context and its doubling count.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces decay by returning to the ballots and attending to area rather than count. A 64-square-inch sheet is halved repeatedly, so each ballot's area is half the previous one, and students look for the pattern relating cuts to area. The What If section has Monroe claim that this decreasing pattern is still an exponential function: students work out what her graph looks like, what equation she wrote, and whether it has a growth factor, growth rate and initial value as the earlier functions did. A second situation gives Zeke's conjecture to test. The problem establishes that decreasing patterns belong to the same family, with a factor less than 1.
entries.approachGuidance: Monroe's and Zeke's claims are for students to evaluate. Support the testing of a claim rather than ruling on it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential decay as a constant factor between 0 and 1; growth factor, growth rate and initial value; writing an equation from a table or graph; percent decrease; that a percent change corresponds to a multiplicative factor.
entries.problemDigest: Names the decay factor and relates it to a decay rate. A dog's 400-milligram dose of flea medicine is tabulated and graphed hour by hour, and students find the factor relating consecutive hours and write an equation linking hours to milligrams remaining. The What If section gives a different medicine breaking down at 20% an hour from a 60-milligram dose and has students extend a table over six hours — which requires turning the 20% rate into a factor of 0.8. Four students' attempts to find that decay factor are then set out for judgement, the common error being to use 0.2 rather than 0.8, so the rate-to-factor relationship is the content under test.
entries.approachGuidance: Four students' reasoning about the decay factor is compared, including incorrect attempts. Help students see why a method fails rather than correcting the number.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential decay, decay factor and decay rate; writing an equation from data; making and reading a graph; that a decay factor lies between 0 and 1; conducting an experiment and tabulating results.
entries.problemDigest: Models decay with real data and finds that the obvious variable does not decay exponentially. Students record boiling water's temperature every five minutes, graph it, describe when it changes fastest and slowest, and decide whether the relationship is exponential decay — it is not, because the temperature levels off at room temperature rather than approaching zero. The What If section supplies the fix: tabulate and graph the difference between water and air temperature instead, which does decay exponentially. A further situation matches decay rates to their corresponding decay factors. This is the unit's clearest case of a model needing adjustment to fit.
entries.approachGuidance: Students' own cooling data will not fit a decay model until the variable is changed, and noticing that is the lesson. Work from their data rather than an idealised curve.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential growth and decay written as y = a(b^x); initial value a and growth or decay factor b; graphs of exponential functions; linear equations in the form y = mx + b and the roles of m and b; graphing several equations on shared axes.
entries.problemDigest: Consolidates by examining how the parameters shape the graph. Students predict and then test how b affects the graph of y = b^x with a fixed at 1, graphing several equations on the same axes and describing the similarities and differences, then repeat with a varying to see what the initial value does. The What If section has students match tables, graphs and scenarios to the equations they graphed, so the parameters must be read out of each representation. The closing question compares the roles of a and b in an exponential equation with those of m and b in a linear one, setting the two families directly against each other.
entries.approachGuidance: Students predict the effect of each parameter before graphing. Support the prediction and the revision of it rather than describing the families of curves.

entries.priorKnowledge: Exponential functions written as y = a(b^n); exponential form, base and exponent; standard and expanded form; scientific notation; from Number Connections, powers of a number; completing and reading a table of values.
entries.problemDigest: Turns from functions to the exponents themselves. Students complete a table of powers of 2 and other whole numbers, describe the patterns they see down the rows and across the columns, explain why each holds, and write a number sentence for each — so the exponent properties are discovered as patterns before being named. The What If section has students judge Roxanne's proof of one conjecture and test whether it works for bases other than 2, consider Federico's observation that some values appear more than once in the table, such as 64 as a power of 2, 4 and 8, and extend the table leftwards into negative exponents, judging classmates' claims about what appears there.
entries.approachGuidance: The properties emerge as student conjectures from a table, several of which are examined. Support conjecture and justification rather than stating the laws.

entries.priorKnowledge: Patterns in a table of powers, including for negative exponents; exponential form; the conjectures raised in 4.1; multiplication as repeated addition of exponents in observed cases; standard and expanded form.
entries.problemDigest: Formalises the exponent properties and asks why they work. Students examine each pattern a class noticed and answer questions about it, moving from observation to justification. The What If section works through Marta's conjecture about a power raised to a power, her reasoning being that (2^3)^2 is (2^3)(2^3), which is 8 × 8, or 8^2 — which also explains Federico's repeated values from 4.1 — and has students apply it to further expressions and say what happens generally when a power is raised to a power. A second situation returns to the negative-exponent conjectures and asks students to show why each holds for any non-zero base.
entries.approachGuidance: The task is to explain why each property holds, not to apply it. Support the justification a student constructs.

entries.priorKnowledge: The exponent properties, including for negative exponents; scientific notation and converting to and from standard form; dividing large numbers; that dividing powers of ten subtracts exponents.
entries.problemDigest: Applies the exponent properties to arithmetic in scientific notation. Finding daily water use per person requires dividing 4.10 × 10^11 gallons by about 330,000,000 people, and two methods are compared: Gary rewrites both numbers in millions, while Julia converts the divisor to 3.30 × 10^8 and divides the powers of ten separately, reasoning that 10^11 ÷ 10^8 is 10^3. The What If section applies the same technique to Illinois water use, including a conversion to gallons per second, examines whether a claim about scientific notation makes sense and whether it was needed, and extends to a further large-number context.
entries.approachGuidance: Gary's and Julia's methods both work and students compare them. Support either route rather than requiring conversion to scientific notation.

entries.priorKnowledge: The exponent properties for integer exponents, including the zero and negative cases; exponential functions and their graphs; reading values off an exponential graph; square roots and cube roots informally.
entries.problemDigest: Extends the exponent properties from integer to rational exponents. An amoeba population quadrupling weekly gives y = 4^x, and students examine observations about patterns in its graph. The What If section then asks for the population after a quarter of a week and after 1.5 weeks, which requires giving meaning to a fractional exponent, and for the time to reach given populations. Three students' interpretations of 16^(3/2) are set out for judgement before students evaluate further rational powers by their own method. A final situation applies the properties to mixed computations. The unit's last problem, extending the rules rather than the functions.
entries.approachGuidance: Three interpretations of a rational exponent are offered and students judge them. Support the sense-making rather than supplying the root-and-power rule.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit: exponential functions as y = a(b^x), with a the initial value and b the growth or decay factor; the relationship between a growth or decay factor and a percent rate; compound growth; doubling time; exponential decay and why some decreasing data needs a changed variable to fit; the effects of a and b on the graph; the exponent properties for integer and rational exponents; scientific notation and arithmetic with it.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's Mathematical Reflections, one per investigation, each asking what students know about exponential functions and expressions and how they compare with linear functions. The expected ground is that an exponential function multiplies by a constant factor where a linear one adds a constant amount; how the initial value and the factor appear in a table, graph and equation; how a factor relates to a percent rate and why growth compounds; what distinguishes decay from growth and what a factor between 0 and 1 means; how a and b shape the graph against m and b in a linear equation; and the exponent properties with the reasoning behind them.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered when the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions — gathered as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. The banks follow the investigations: recognising exponential growth in tables, graphs and equations and distinguishing it from linear growth, with exponential and scientific notation; working with fractional growth factors, percent growth rates, compound growth and doubling time; exponential decay, decay factors and rates, and fitting a decay model to data; and the exponent properties for integer, zero, negative and rational exponents together with arithmetic in scientific notation. This is the unit's largest item by a wide margin and is individual practice on content introduced elsewhere.
